tips: Watch for the formula "that it might be fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22; 2:15; 4:14). Matthew writes for readers who know the Old Testament and shows Jesus as the one it pointed to.
Notice the five long blocks of teaching, each ending with words like "when Jesus had ended these sayings" (Matthew 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). The first is the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7).
Follow the theme of "the kingdom of heaven," Matthew's favorite phrase. Many parables begin "The kingdom of heaven is like…" (Matthew 13).

looksBack.title: Son of David, son of Abraham
looksBack.text: The opening genealogy (Matthew 1:1–17) ties Jesus to the promises made to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and David (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

looksBack.title: A new Moses
looksBack.text: Like Moses, the infant Jesus escapes a king's massacre, comes out of Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15), and teaches God's will from a mountain (Matthew 5:1).

looksAhead.title: The Great Commission
looksAhead.text: Matthew ends with Jesus sending his disciples to "teach all nations" (Matthew 28:19–20); Acts tells how that mission began.

looksAhead.title: The other Gospels
looksAhead.text: Much of Matthew's material is shared with Mark and Luke; comparing the accounts shows what each writer emphasizes.

tips: Read it quickly, perhaps in one sitting. It is the shortest and most action-filled Gospel; the word "straightway" (immediately) appears again and again.
Notice the turning point at Peter's confession, "Thou art the Christ" (Mark 8:29). After it, Jesus begins to teach plainly that he must suffer, die, and rise again (Mark 8:31).

Watch for what scholars call the messianic secret. Jesus often tells people not to speak about who he is, because his identity can only be understood through the cross—the first human in Mark to declare him the Son of God is a Roman centurion watching him die (Mark 15:39).

looksBack.title: The voice in the wilderness
looksBack.text: Mark opens by quoting the prophets (Mark 1:2–3; Malachi 3:1; Isaiah 40:3) to introduce John the Baptist as the one preparing the Lord's way.

looksAhead.title: Peter's preaching
looksAhead.text: Peter's summary of Jesus' ministry in Acts 10:36–43, from John's baptism to the resurrection, follows the same outline as Mark's Gospel.

looksAhead.title: A ransom for many
looksAhead.text: Jesus' words that he came "to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) are developed in the letters, such as 1 Timothy 2:5–6.

tips: Read the preface (Luke 1:1–4). Luke writes as a careful historian so that Theophilus may know "the certainty of those things" he has been taught.

Notice the people Luke highlights: the poor, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, and sinners. Many parables found only in Luke, such as the good Samaritan and the prodigal son (Luke 10; 15), show God's welcome to outsiders.
Follow the long journey to Jerusalem that begins when Jesus "stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51). Much of the Gospel's teaching is given on the road.

looksBack.title: Back to Adam
looksBack.text: Luke's genealogy runs all the way back to "Adam, which was the son of God" (Luke 3:23–38), presenting Jesus as Savior for all humanity.

looksBack.title: All the scriptures
looksBack.text: After the resurrection, Jesus explains how "Moses and all the prophets" spoke of him (Luke 24:27, 44).

looksAhead.title: Volume two
looksAhead.text: Acts continues Luke's account, picking up with the ascension (Acts 1:1–11; Luke 24:50–53) and the promise of the Spirit.

tips: Start with the prologue (John 1:1–18). It tells you who Jesus is before the story begins: the eternal Word who "was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
Watch for the seven signs—miracles such as turning water into wine (John 2:11) and raising Lazarus (chapter 11)—and the seven "I am" sayings, such as "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35).
Notice how much of the book covers Jesus' last week. Chapters 13–17 record his long farewell talk with the disciples on the night before he died.

looksBack.title: In the beginning
looksBack.text: John's opening words, "In the beginning" (John 1:1), deliberately echo Genesis 1:1.

looksBack.title: I AM
looksBack.text: Jesus' words "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) recall the name God gave Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14).

looksAhead.title: John's letters
looksAhead.text: 1 John echoes the Gospel's themes and language—light, life, love, and truth—beginning with "that which was from the beginning" (1 John 1:1).

looksAhead.title: The Lamb of God
looksAhead.text: John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29); Revelation pictures him as the Lamb on the throne (Revelation 5:6–12).

tips: Use Acts 1:8 as the book's map: the gospel spreads "in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." The story follows that outward movement.
Notice the shift in focus from Peter (chapters 1–12) to Paul (13–28). Following Paul's three missionary journeys on a map makes the second half easier to follow.
Pay attention to the speeches—Peter's at Pentecost (chapter 2), Stephen's (chapter 7), Paul's in Athens (chapter 17). They show how the earliest believers explained the gospel.

looksBack.title: The promise of the Father
looksBack.text: Acts begins where Luke ends, with Jesus telling the disciples to wait for the promised Spirit (Acts 1:4–5; Luke 24:49).

looksBack.title: Babel reversed
looksBack.text: At Pentecost people from many nations hear the gospel in their own languages (Acts 2:5–11), a reversal of the scattering at Babel (Genesis 11:7–9).

looksAhead.title: Paul's letters
looksAhead.text: Many of Paul's letters were written to churches founded in Acts, such as Philippi (Acts 16), Thessalonica (Acts 17:1–9), Corinth (Acts 18), and Ephesus (Acts 19).

looksAhead.title: An unfinished ending
looksAhead.text: Acts ends with Paul in Rome, preaching "with all confidence, no man forbidding him" (Acts 28:30–31), leaving the story open for the church to continue.
